questions.text: What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling, and when would you choose each?
questions.answer: "Vertical scaling means making one machine bigger — more CPU, RAM, faster disk. Horizontal means adding more machines behind a router. Vertical is cheaper to implement because there's no coordination, no data movement, and no new code — it's the right first move, and it stays the right move as long as your data fits in RAM and one machine can handle the write throughput. Horizontal is what you need when you exceed one machine's capacity, or when you need redundancy — and you need redundancy almost immediately, because a single machine, however big, is a single point of failure no matter how much RAM it has. So in practice: vertical for the database while it's small, and horizontal for the stateless tier from day one, because adding app servers is cheaper than a bigger app server."

questions.text: Explain load balancing algorithms. Which would you use and why?
questions.answer: "There are about seven worth knowing. Round-robin: next server in rotation — fine for homogeneous servers with cheap requests, bad when request cost varies. Weighted round-robin: when servers differ in size. Least-connections: send to the server with the fewest active connections — good for long-lived connections. Least-outstanding-requests: fewest in-flight requests — this is what I'd usually use, because it's the most accurate signal of load and it self-corrects. IP or consistent hashing for sticky sessions — I'd avoid it, it destroys the ability to replace a failed server. Power-of-two-random-choices for very large fleets of cheap workers, because it needs no shared state. And least-latency for heterogeneous fleets. The algorithm is less important than the health check. I'd use least-outstanding-requests behind an L7 balancer with passive outlier detection, so a partially-broken server gets ejected based on observed errors rather than a health check. And I'd never add sticky sessions to hide a statefulness bug — it prevents failover and blocks rolling deploys."

questions.text: What is a stateless service and why does it matter?
questions.answer: "A stateless service keeps no request-specific state in the process. It matters because statelessness is the precondition for horizontal scaling, for replacing a failed instance instantly, for rolling deploys without dropping sessions, and for autoscaling — all of which need the ability to send a request to any instance. Getting there means inventorying the state: identity state goes into a signed cookie or a session store; cacheable state goes into a bounded local cache with a short TTL; durable state goes into the database with an idempotency key; and file state goes into object storage. The discipline is that any local cache is only acceptable for something a user would call 'slightly wrong' — never for anything they'd call 'lost money' or 'wrong permission'."

questions.text: How do you invalidate a CDN cache?
questions.answer: "The primary mechanism should be content-addressed URLs — if the content changes, the URL changes, so there's nothing to invalidate. That works great for static assets like JS and images, which are immutable by construction, and lets you set a one-year max-age with immutable. For everything else, I'd use short TTLs as the base guarantee and purge only as a targeted tool. The CDNs that scale do purge by tag — you tag objects with a surrogate key like /users/42/avatar and purge the tag, which is the only purge design that survives fan-out. A per-URL purge API melts under load. The most valuable headers are actually stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error — they turn the cache from a performance optimization into an availability mechanism, because users get instant stale content instead of an error when the origin is slow or down. The two things that break CDN caching are Set-Cookie on responses, which makes them uncacheable by default, and Vary headers — every value of a varied header multiplies your object count and fragments your hit rate."

questions.text: When would you add read replicas, and what's the risk?
questions.answer: "When reads dominate writes — typically a read:write ratio of 100:1 or more — replicas are almost always the right next step, because they multiply read capacity roughly linearly and cost nothing in coordination. The risk is read-your-writes. If a user updates their profile and the next GET hits a replica with a second of lag, they see the old value, and users report that as a bug even though 'eventually consistent' is technically true. The mitigations are: route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write, use a per-user sticky route for a bounded time, or pass a minimum version and have the replica wait until it has applied that version. The second risk is failover. If the primary dies and you promote an asynchronous replica, you lose every acknowledged-but-not-replicated write. So replicas are a read-scaling tool, and if you need RPO=0 you need synchronous replication — which is a different design with a write latency cost."

questions.text: What is the connection pool problem with Postgres and how do you solve it?
questions.answer: "Postgres creates an OS process per connection, roughly 5–10 MB each, and its default max_connections is 100. With 200 app instances times 20 connections, you have 4,000 backend processes. That's tens of gigabytes of memory spent on processes that are mostly idle, plus scheduler and context-switch thrash. Postgres also performs badly when connection count exceeds roughly two to four times core count — the lock manager and scheduler become the bottleneck before CPU does. The fix is a connection proxy: PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a few dozen server connections. Transaction mode means it returns the server connection after each transaction, which requires that your app not rely on session state — no LISTEN/NOTIFY across transactions, no temp tables, no advisory locks held across a transaction, no SET that isn't reset. If you need query-aware routing, caching, or read/write splitting, ProxySQL does that. The mental model I use: don't think of 'as many connections as possible' — think of 'a small number of connections per instance, behind a proxy that multiplexes.'"

questions.text: Explain partitioning vs sharding.
questions.answer: "Partitioning splits one table inside one database into many physical tables. It prunes I/O and enables instant retention — dropping a monthly partition instead of deleting two billion rows — but it doesn't increase write throughput beyond one instance, and it can hurt, because more tables means more planning overhead and more open files. Sharding splits data across multiple database instances. Now you're horizontal, and you've crossed a one-way door: no joins across shards, no cross-shard transactions, rebalancing is a multi-day operation, and unique constraints become unique-within-a-shard. The decision rule is access pattern and lifecycle. If queries are time-bounded or you need retention, partition by time. If one machine can't hold the data or can't take the writes, shard by hash or by tenant. And you should pick the shard key by the dominant query, not by even distribution — shard by whatever the queries read by, so those queries stay local."

questions.text: Why is modulo-based sharding a problem, and what is consistent hashing?
questions.answer: "Modulo sharding has the property that changing N reshuffles almost everything. Going from 8 shards to 9 means only about one in nine keys land on the same shard, so you're migrating essentially your entire dataset — offline — for a resize. That makes the shard count effectively fixed forever, which is unacceptable. Consistent hashing puts nodes and keys on a ring by hash, so adding or removing a node only moves roughly 1/N of the keys. But vanilla consistent hashing has bad load balance, because each node owns one big random arc. The fix is virtual nodes: give each physical node 100 to 500 points on the ring, so its share concentrates tightly around 1/N. There's a subtlety worth knowing: real systems like Dynamo use ranged hashing — contiguous ranges of the ring assigned to nodes — because that gives you range scans, natural replicas per range, and the ability to split a single hot range. And for small N, rendezvous or highest-random-weight hashing is simpler and provably moves the minimal number of keys with no ring to maintain."

questions.text: What are virtual nodes and why do you need them?
questions.answer: "In consistent hashing, each node occupies one arc of the ring, and those arcs are random variables. With three nodes it's quite likely one node gets 70% of the ring. That's a real load-imbalance problem, and you can't fix it after the fact. Virtual nodes solve it: each physical node registers 100 to 500 points on the ring, so it owns 100 to 500 small arcs. The law of large numbers concentrates each node's total share tightly around 1/N, so the variance collapses. With 5 nodes and 256 vnodes each, the maximum deviation from perfect balance is a few percent. The practical requirements: the vnode set must be computable identically by every node, so the hash function, node identity, and vnode index all have to be agreed on; and you should make the vnodes-per-node a parameter, so you can tune the ratio without re-adding all nodes."

questions.text: What is backpressure and load shedding?
questions.answer: "Backpressure is a mechanism for a slow consumer to slow down a fast producer, so that a throughput problem doesn't become a latency problem and then an out-of-memory problem. The simplest and most important form is a bounded queue — every queue must have a max size, and on overflow you either block the producer or reject. Beyond that: caller-runs semantics, reactive streams' demand-driven flow control, credit-based flow control like Kafka and gRPC, and adaptive concurrency limits. Load shedding is deliberately dropping or deferring work so a subset of users gets a fast failure instead of everyone getting a slow one. The patterns in increasing order of politeness: cap in-flight requests at the edge; shed low-priority work first — analytics, prefetch, background — to protect the user-facing path; propagate deadlines so a downstream hop doesn't work on a request nobody is waiting for; and have a documented degradation ladder that says what to drop first. The reason this matters is queueing theory: past the knee, adding work makes things worse for everyone, and overload collapse is worse than overload. Retries make it far worse, which is why clients need backoff with full jitter and a retry budget."

questions.text: What's the difference between CPU-based and queue-depth-based autoscaling?
questions.answer: "CPU is a lagging proxy. For an HTTP service handling variable-cost requests, CPU reflects utilization, not demand — and by the time CPU is high, latency is already climbing. But CPU is stable and cheap to measure, which is why it's the default. Queue depth is the truth for asynchronous workers. If you have a backlog of 1 million messages, adding CPU only helps if the bottleneck is CPU; if it's an external API rate limit, more consumers just make the throttling worse. So scale queue consumers on backlog count or, better, on the age of the oldest message — because a shrinking backlog of slow-to-process messages is still a latency violation. For latency-sensitive APIs, neither is great: concurrency or in-flight requests is the signal that predicts latency. And for known patterns — a 9am traffic spike, a game launch — scheduled or predictive scaling gets capacity in place before the spike, with reactive scaling as the backstop. The biggest real-world gotcha in all of this is cold start: image pull plus JIT warmup plus cache fill means a new instance is useless for 30 to 90 seconds, so reactive scaling inherently loses the first minutes of every spike."

questions.text: Active-active vs active-passive?
questions.answer: "Active-passive is simpler: one region writes, the other is a hot standby. You get clean consistency because there's a single writer, and failover is a routing switch. The costs are that you pay for idle capacity, and failover takes as long as promotion plus DNS propagation — think minutes — and you're regionally vulnerable the whole time. Active-active gives every region local latency and no failover event at all, because no region failing is a failure. The cost is that write conflict resolution becomes your problem: you either route writes to a home region per entity, or you accept last-write-wins and lose concurrent writes, or you go full multi-master with vector clocks and reconciliation. The decision is fundamentally latency versus consistency. Strict consistency across continents means every write pays 70 to 150 milliseconds of extra RTT. So my default is: single region or active-passive until the latency SLO forces otherwise, then active-active with a home region per entity and a defined consistency budget per operation."

questions.text: Explain the CAP theorem properly.
questions.answer: "The precise statement is: in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. Two things it's often misquoted as: it doesn't say you can't have both C and A — you can, whenever there's no partition — and it doesn't say you choose at design time; the choice only exists during a partition, which is usually rare. The more useful refinement for engineers is PACELC: if there's a Partition, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. That matters because the latency-versus-consistency trade exists on every single normal request, while the CAP trade only exists during the rare partition. So the practical design is: in steady state, choose low latency with bounded staleness; during a partition, choose per operation — CP for money and permissions, AP for likes and presence — and have an explicit reconciliation story for the AP parts."

questions.text: Is your design CP or AP?
questions.answer: "That question doesn't have an answer for a system as a whole, so let me be specific per operation. Payments, idempotency-key registration, permissions, and seat reservation are CP — I reject on the minority side rather than risk a double-spend or a permission violation. Likes, view counts, presence, and recommendations are AP — every replica accepts, and I reconcile with read-repair and counters. Reads are local with a stated staleness bound, which is a PACELC 'E' choice, not a CAP choice. The thing I want to be explicit about is that 'AP' is not a free pass. If two replicas accept writes concurrently and you have no conflict-resolution strategy, AP is just data loss. So every AP write path in my design names what happens on conflict — usually a hybrid logical clock with last-write-wins for scalars, or read-repair plus a sibling for anything a user would notice."

questions.text: Explain consensus (Raft) at a level you can defend.
questions.answer: "Consensus lets a set of nodes agree on a totally ordered log despite crashes, message loss, and reordering, with no shared memory and no reliable clock. It's only useful for small, critical coordination state — service discovery, config, locks, membership, sequence allocation — because consensus plus state-machine replication means every write pays a round trip before it's acknowledged. The 2f+1 rule: five nodes tolerate two failures. The mechanics are a leader that orders operations and replicates them in parallel, committing once a majority has stored an entry, then applying to a deterministic state machine. Followers that stop hearing from the leader start a randomized election timeout and become candidates; winning a majority makes you leader. The safety argument is three rules. Election restriction: a candidate can only win if its log is at least as up to date as a majority's, which implies a leader's log contains every committed entry. Log matching: if two logs share an index and term, they're identical up to that point. And leader completeness follows from those two. Liveness needs randomized timeouts, because the FLP result says deterministic consensus can't guarantee termination in an async system with even one crash. Read paths need care: the correct approach is ReadIndex — confirm leadership by exchanging heartbeats, then read locally without a log round trip. Lease-based reads are faster but depend on clock bounds, and clocks lie."

questions.text: What is a split brain and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: "Split-brain is two nodes each acting as authoritative leader. The causes are: a network partition where each side believes it has a majority; a lease that expires because the holder was GC-paused or frozen, and which resumes still believing it holds the lease; clock skew making a TTL look valid on two nodes; and stale routing sending traffic to both. Prevention is layered. First, quorum intersection — never make a safety decision on a minority, so 2f+1 nodes and quorum-based election. Second, fencing tokens: the leader gets a monotonically increasing token from the coordination store, and every write to the protected resource carries it and is rejected if it's lower than the highest seen. That's the important one, because it converts a correctness problem into an availability problem — a stale leader does no damage regardless of what it believes. Third, longer TTLs with margin, and don't suspend the leader process. Fourth, make the side effect itself idempotent, so a double-run is harmless."

questions.text: What is an idempotency key and when do you need it?
questions.answer: "Any time a retry could duplicate a side effect, you need one. The pattern: the client generates a key, the server stores the key, the request hash, and the response, and does the insert in the same transaction as the business write. A retry finds the key and replays the stored response verbatim, so the user gets the same answer, not just the same effect. The details that matter: scope the key per user and endpoint, store a hash of the request body so a mismatched reuse is a 422, keep keys for longer than your retry window, and — this is the bug everyone makes — the key record has to be committed in the same transaction as the work, or you can record a key and then fail the work, and every retry says 'already done' for something that never happened. You need it for payments, order placement, reservations, signup, webhook receivers, and message consumers. And where you have a database and a message broker, the transactional outbox is the companion pattern: write the change and an outbox row in one transaction, then relay to the broker, and let idempotent consumers handle at-least-once delivery."

questions.text: What is the Transactional Outbox pattern and why?
questions.answer: "You need to write to your database and publish to a message broker atomically, and you can't — they're separate systems with no shared transaction. The naive options both lose data: write DB then publish risks losing the message if you crash in between; publish then write DB risks a duplicate message and a phantom event. The outbox pattern: in one database transaction, update the aggregate and insert a row into an outbox table. A separate relay polls the outbox — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so multiple relays can run — publishes to Kafka, and marks rows as published. Delivery is at-least-once, and consumers are idempotent, so effectively-once. The cost is polling latency and an extra table that needs cleanup. The lower-latency alternative is CDC: read the database's WAL directly with something like Debezium, so there's no polling interval. Either way, consumer idempotency is mandatory, because at-least-once is the only guarantee you'll get."

questions.text: What is a saga, and choreography vs orchestration?
questions.answer: "A saga decomposes a distributed transaction into local transactions, each with a compensating action, coordinated by messages or by a central orchestrator. There's no blocking and no 2PC, so you get availability instead of atomicity, and you pay in eventual consistency and visible intermediate states. Choreography is event-driven: each service subscribes and reacts, the flow is implicit in code. It decouples beautifully and there's no bottleneck, but the flow becomes invisible — nobody can answer 'what happens if step four fails' without reading five codebases — and as participants grow it becomes event spaghetti. Orchestration has a central coordinator that holds a durable state machine and issues commands. The flow is explicit and versioned, timeouts and SLAs are centralized, long-running and human-in-the- loop steps are natural, and it's far easier to test. My rule: orchestration when it's a procedure with business meaning — checkout, provisioning, fulfillment, anything involving money. Choreography when it's a set of independent reactions — notify, index, cache, analytics. And two things that matter more than the choice: compensation is not rollback, it's a new forward action, like a refund as a new credit entry in an append-only ledger; and you should do the irreversible step last, so you charge after you reserve, not before."

questions.text: Why not just use 2PC for distributed transactions?
questions.answer: "Because 2PC is blocking. Participants that have voted prepare must wait for the coordinator's decision. If the coordinator crashes, or if the network partitions between the coordinator and a participant, those participants hold their locks and block — potentially for the lifetime of the transaction. A single coordinator failure becomes a database-wide lock storm. On top of that, a commit costs two to three round trips inside the critical path, and the coordinator is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure. The practical answer is that you don't need cross-system atomicity as often as you think you do. Spend the transactional guarantee on one store you control — Postgres, or a Spanner — and treat cross-service state as eventually consistent via the outbox pattern plus a saga with compensation. Where 2PC is acceptable is inside a cluster you own, on a small homogeneous group of replicas, which is exactly what etcd and ZooKeeper do internally: consensus over one replicated log, never two-phase commit across heterogeneous external systems."

questions.text: Explain read-your-writes and how you implement it.
questions.answer: "Read-your-writes means a client never sees a state older than its own write. It's the consistency guarantee users actually notice, and it's the one that breaks when you introduce replicas. There are three implementations, in increasing order of cost. One: route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write — simple, but couples reads to the primary and hurts read scalability for heavy writers. Two: per-user sticky routing for a bounded window. Three, the best general one: put a version or ETag in the write response, let the client send min_version on subsequent reads, and have the replica wait — with a short timeout — until it has applied that version, then fall back to the primary if it can't catch up. In the API I'd make this explicit rather than hidden: return the version in every write response, accept it as a read parameter, and let callers choose. That way freshness is a contract rather than an accident."

questions.text: Why can't we have consistent, available, and low-latency systems?
questions.answer: "Because of the speed of light and because consistency requires agreement. If two clients write concurrently and both must see the writes in the same order, then before the second write can be acknowledged, the system must know the first write's outcome — which means either the second client waits for a round trip to the first, or the system uses a leader and the write is serialized through it. Concretely: a linearizable write acknowledged to a client in region A must be visible to a subsequent read in region B. That's a round trip to region B, or the write must be synchronously replicated there — which is the same round trip, about 70 to 150 milliseconds across an ocean. You can have consistency and availability, but only by paying latency. You can have low latency and availability, but only by accepting staleness. Consistency and low latency together require you to be in one place — which is why single-region systems can be both fast and consistent, and why global systems pick which one they give up."

questions.text: What are the consistency models, and which would you use where?
questions.answer: "From strongest: linearizable — operations appear to take effect instantaneously, which you get with consensus; sequential — all nodes see the same order but not necessarily real-time order; causal — causally related operations are seen in order everywhere, which needs vector clocks; then read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes, which are session-level guarantees; then eventual consistency, which converges; and bounded staleness, which is eventual with a time bound. The practical advice is: set the consistency requirement per operation, per field, not per system. Payments, inventory commit, permissions, and uniqueness checks are linearizable. User profiles are bounded-stale at about a second, or read-your-writes. Feeds, likes, and search are eventual with a stated bound. Analytics is batch. And remember that read consistency is a separate choice from write consistency — that's the trap when you add replicas. N writes to the primary and reads from replicas means your read consistency is exactly your replication lag, whether you designed for it or not."

questions.text: Explain timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and hedging.
questions.answer: "These are the four controls on failure, and they work at different layers. Timeouts bound the wait. Every call needs one. And critically, propagate deadlines rather than timeouts — pass an absolute deadline downstream so a hop with 40 milliseconds left doesn't start a 100-millisecond query. Set timeouts around p99.9 of the dependency, always less than the caller's own timeout. Retries handle transient failure, with three rules: only retry idempotent operations, use exponential backoff with full jitter — the jitter is what breaks synchronization — and cap retries with a budget, around 10 percent of requests, so the system always has capacity for first-time traffic. Also, pick one retry layer; app plus SDK plus service mesh is three to the third, which is 27 attempts. Circuit breakers fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy. Their real value isn't saving the error, it's freeing up threads and connections so the rest of your service can keep working. Scope them per dependency and per call site. Hedging fixes tail latency: after p95, send a second request to a different replica and take the first success. On a heavy-tailed latency distribution the second request has an independent chance of being fast, so p99 improves a lot for about 5 to 10 percent extra load. Only hedge below a load threshold, though — doubling load during an incident is exactly when you can't afford it."

questions.text: How do you choose a timeout?
questions.answer: "Three inputs. First, the dependency's own latency distribution under normal load — I want around p99.9, not the max, because a max-based timeout either fires on legitimate tail events or never fires. Second, my own remaining deadline: the timeout must be shorter than the caller's budget, leaving room for me to return my own error, which is much better for the user than a generic gateway timeout. Third, the cost of waiting versus the cost of failing — if the call is optional, like recommendations, a short timeout and skip is right; if it's required, a longer timeout is right. The trap is a single global timeout. Different operations need different values: a metadata lookup at 100 milliseconds, a search at one second, a batch export at a minute. And the other trap is unbounded waits — no timeout at all turns one slow dependency into thread-pool exhaustion and a whole-service outage."

questions.text: What is a bulkhead and why do you need one?
questions.answer: "A bulkhead is a resource pool per dependency or feature, so one starving resource can't consume everything. It's named after ship compartments for a reason. Concretely: a separate thread pool and connection pool per downstream service, so the search service's 4-second latency can't exhaust the threads that checkout needs. Shuffle-sharding across per-tenant pools so a noisy tenant can't starve others. And the strongest bulkhead is a separate deployment — if recommendations are in their own service and their own pods, their failure can't touch checkout at all, which no in-process pool achieves. In one outage I worked through, a search dependency went slow, exhausted a shared 200-thread pool, and took down checkout, profile, and everything else — one slow dependency, whole-service outage. Bulkheads are the structural fix: the pool for search had 10 threads, search degraded to returning nothing, and checkout never noticed."

questions.text: How do you rate limit at scale?
questions.answer: "Token bucket is the algorithm I'd default to — tokens refill at a rate, the bucket holds a burst allowance, and each request takes one. It allows controlled bursts while enforcing the long-term average, which is what APIs need. The important design decision is that you limit cost, not requests. A search costs ten times a read, so a request-count limit doesn't control resource consumption. I use hierarchical limits — per-user, per-tenant, and global — and reject if any is exceeded. For distribution, the two-layer approach: a local token bucket in each instance for the hot path, with no network hop, plus a global bucket in Redis for fairness across instances, enforced with an atomic Lua script so check-and-decrement can't race. Also do per-IP limiting at the CDN or edge, which absorbs volumetric abuse for free. Two operational notes: always return 429 with Retry-After, or clients hammer. And the limiter itself must be protected — if Redis fails, decide per endpoint whether you fail open for availability or fail closed for security, and have a local fallback."

questions.text: What are CRDTs and when would you use one?
questions.answer: "A CRDT is a data type whose replicas can be updated without coordination and still converge to the same value. The theory is that convergence comes from three properties — commutativity, associativity, and idempotency — and if your merge operation has all three, replicas converge regardless of order or duplication. The canonical use is collaborative text, where last-write-wins would lose one person's edits. Each character insertion gets a unique causally-ordered ID, and all replicas merge the set of insertions by that order. That's the basis of CRDT-based editors and offline-first apps. Where I'd be careful: CRDTs converge, but they don't necessarily converge to something correct for the business. They can't enforce arbitrary invariants like balance ≥ 0 or capacity ≤ 100. And a scalar that two users set to different values isn't a technical conflict — it's a product conflict that sometimes needs a human. So: CRDT for user-visible collaborative conflicts, bounded staleness for ordinary reads, strong consistency for money. And CRDT metadata needs causality-tracked garbage collection, which is a distributed-systems problem in itself."

questions.text: How do you handle ordering without a global clock?
questions.answer: "You first decide what order you actually need. Most systems don't need a global total order — they need per-entity order, like per conversation or per feed. So assign a per-entity sequence number at ingest, from a database sequence, a Redis increment, or the Kafka partition offset, and let clients dedupe and reorder. That's cheap and correct for the requirement. When you do need cross-node causality, Lamport clocks give you a consistent order that respects happens-before, but they can't detect concurrency — equal counters mean concurrent. Vector clocks detect concurrency precisely but cost metadata proportional to node count. For real systems the best modern answer is hybrid logical clocks, which produce timestamps that are both causally ordered and close to physical time, so TTLs and human-readable timestamps still work. And for correctness decisions, never trust a wall clock across machines — use HLC, a database version, or a consensus log index. The rule I hold to: wall clocks are for humans and for TTLs with slack; they're never the sole basis for a correctness decision."

questions.text: What is a lease and what's the lease problem?
questions.answer: "A lease says 'you may act as leader for a fixed duration, and the grantor expires it after that.' The problem is that you cannot make a lease safe with clocks alone. For safety you need bounded clock skew, you need the holder never to pause longer than the TTL margin, and you need the resource to validate the lease. Any one of those failing means two nodes can both believe they hold it. The mitigations are: conservative TTLs sized as a multiple of maximum clock skew plus maximum expected pause; avoiding process suspension for the leader; and — the real fix — fencing tokens. The coordination store hands out a monotonically increasing number with the lease, every operation carries it, and the protected resource rejects anything lower than the highest it's seen. That makes safety independent of clocks, because a stale leader simply can't do damage no matter what it believes."

questions.text: How do you detect that a node is down?
questions.answer: "You can't prove it's down, so you estimate. There are three approaches. Active heartbeats are simple and fast, but they have two failure modes: a frozen process keeps answering heartbeats, and a network blip makes a live node look dead — which is what causes split-brain. Passive detection is more robust in practice: clients observe errors and latency to a peer and eject it after N failures or a failure rate over a window. It needs no cooperation, and it only detects failures you actually hit. Suspicion is the best of both, and it's what Cassandra and Dynamo use. Track heartbeat inter-arrival as an EWMA; when it exceeds a threshold, mark the node suspected, not dead; gossip that suspicion; and only confirm when others agree. Cassandra formalizes this as the PHI accrual failure detector, which converts the inter-arrival distribution into a probability and adapts the threshold to current network conditions. The distinction between suspected and dead is what prevents a transient congestion event from cascading into a mass ejection."

questions.text: What is quorum and what's the R + W > N rule?
questions.answer: "With N replicas, a write goes to W and a read returns from R. If R + W > N, the read quorum and the write quorum must overlap, so the read is guaranteed to see the write. With N=3, W=2, R=2 works; W=1, R=1 doesn't, and can return stale data. Two caveats worth stating, because the rule is often quoted without them. First, in real systems reads are often 'sloppy quorum' — the coordinator returns a value from any live replica, possibly stale, to satisfy the read — so R+W>N alone doesn't guarantee much when you can partition. Second, the practical cost is that a quorum write is as slow as its slowest replica, and a quorum read is as slow as the R-th fastest, not the fastest. So W=3 against a slow replica makes every write as slow as that replica. In practice most systems aren't quorum systems at all — they're single-leader replication, which is simpler and gives ordering, and they use quorum reasoning for the leaderless Dynamo-style stores. Quorums are the right tool for counters, where losing an increment is unacceptable."

questions.text: Your cache is down. What happens and what do you do?
questions.answer: "It becomes a load multiplier, not a load-neutral event. If you had a 97 percent hit rate at 15,000 QPS, you were sending 450 QPS to the database. Now you're sending all 15,000 — and because a cache-aside miss on a 50-item page becomes 50 item reads, you might be looking at 750,000 reads a second against a database sized for tens of thousands. The response, in order: open the circuit breaker on Redis so retries stop; deliberately shed — accept maybe 2,000 QPS and reject the rest with 503 and Retry-After; serve from any local in-process cache you have; disable non-essential features to reduce query load; and cap database connections so the origin can't be taken down too. For recovery, don't warm the cache at full rate — you'll stampede again. Warm gradually, add jittered TTLs, and enable single-flight. And structurally: the reason this hurts so much is that your hit rate is doing the load-bearing work and the miss path is untested. Test it. Also, a local cache in front of Redis is worth a lot here, because it survives a Redis outage."

questions.text: What's the difference between throughput and latency, and why do they trade off?
questions.answer: "Throughput is work per second; latency is time per unit of work. You can raise one without the other: batching raises both, caching raises throughput a lot and latency somewhat, and adding servers raises throughput but leaves per-request latency roughly flat until you cross the knee. They trade off through utilization. As utilization approaches one, response time goes up non-linearly — for an M/M/1 queue, latency is roughly service time divided by one minus utilization, so at 99 percent utilization you're waiting about a hundred times the service time. That's why you add capacity before the knee, not after, and why a system past the knee can get *worse* when you add load. The practical consequence is Little's Law: concurrency equals throughput times latency. At 2,000 QPS and 100 milliseconds you're holding about 200 concurrent requests. That's how you turn a latency problem into a connection-pool problem, which is how you turn a latency problem into an outage."

questions.text: Design a rate limiter that survives Redis being down.
questions.answer: "Two layers. A local token bucket in every instance, so there's always something enforcing a limit with no network hop; and a global bucket in Redis for fairness across instances. Requests must pass both, and the local bucket is what actually sheds load spikes while Redis is degraded. For Redis failure, fail open with a local fallback rate rather than failing closed, unless the endpoint is security-sensitive, in which case fail closed. And return 429 with Retry-After plus the standard RateLimit-* headers, because clients that don't know when to back off just hammer. Two details people miss: the check-and-decrement must be atomic, so a Lua script or a transaction — otherwise you over-admit under concurrency. And rate-limit cost, not request count, or a tenant running one very expensive query a second still destroys you."

questions.text: Explain read replicas, connection proxies, caching, sharding, and partitioning — when would you use each?
questions.answer: "In increasing order of cost. Caching hides reads — cache-aside with a TTL, plus single-flight to stop stampedes, and it's the right first move for hot, recomputable data. Read replicas multiply read capacity roughly linearly, and the risk is read-your-writes, which you handle with routing or version fences. Connection proxies solve a problem people forget: Postgres connection counts, not query capacity, is often the limit, and PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes thousands of clients onto dozens of backends. Partitioning splits one table to prune I/O and make retention instant via dropping a monthly partition — but it doesn't buy write throughput. Sharding splits across instances and does buy write throughput and capacity, at the cost of no joins, no cross-shard transactions, and painful rebalancing. The order I actually follow is: fix the query, cache, replicas, vertical scale, denormalize, a connection proxy, then partition, then shard. Most 'scale to a billion users' answers skip straight to sharding, and they're wrong — a billion users often just needed an index."

questions.text: What is the two-request model for CDNs and why does it matter?
questions.answer: "A cache miss costs two RTTs and exposes your origin: the edge forwards to origin, waits, caches, and serves. One un-cacheable hot object therefore becomes a self-inflicted DDoS, because every request pays full origin latency and origin bandwidth. Mitigations, in order: make things cacheable in the first place — the single biggest lever is getting Cache-Control right. Use a shield or mid-tier so N simultaneous misses for one object become one origin fetch. Use cache collaboration so POPs share fills. And use signed URLs or signed cookies so you can cache personalized content without caching per-user variants. The operational consequence is that a cache purge is a miss storm. So purge by tag, not by URL; prefer soft purge — mark stale and revalidate — over hard purge; and prefer versioned URLs so invalidation isn't needed at all."

questions.text: How do you handle a dependency that's slow but not down?
questions.answer: "Slow is worse than down, because down fails fast and slow consumes resources. A dependency at 4 seconds with 15,000 QPS means 60,000 concurrent in-flight requests, which exhausts your thread pool in milliseconds and takes down every endpoint sharing it — that's the cascading failure. The fixes: a short timeout plus deadline propagation so the hop fails fast rather than working on a request nobody is waiting for; a circuit breaker with a slow-call-rate threshold, not just an error threshold; a bulkhead so the slowness is contained; and, best, make the dependency async or precomputed — if recommendations don't need to be real-time, don't call them in the request. And I'd raise a generic point: alert on dependency latency independently of errors, because slowness is a leading indicator and errors are a lagging one. By the time you're seeing errors, the queue is already full and the recovery is much slower."

questions.text: What's your approach to a schema migration on a large table?
questions.answer: "Expand-contract, always. First release adds the new column as nullable, or adds the new table, while the old code keeps working. Second, backfill — but in batches, with a rate limit, because a single 500-million-row update generates enormous WAL, blocks, and can take the table offline. Third, dual-write: new writes go to both old and new. Fourth, verify with a comparison job. Fifth, switch reads to the new. Sixth, remove the old path in a later release, after usage telemetry confirms nothing reads it. The discipline is that every intermediate state must be correct and independently shippable, because you never get to do all six steps at once — a deploy, an incident, or a schema revert will interleave. And on a sharded table, you also have to roll the migration across every shard, which means a migration orchestrator that tracks per-shard state."

questions.text: What would you do differently at 100× the current scale?
questions.answer: "Separating two kinds of problems: capacity problems, which are solvable with money, and decision problems, which are not. Capacity: the storage and bandwidth numbers grow 100× and are handled by object storage and CDN — that part never needs redesign. Read QPS grows 100× and is handled by the stateless tier and the cache. Those are budgeting problems. Decisions: the shard key, the consistency model per operation, and the cache key design are the three things that are expensive or impossible to change later. So those are what I need to get right now, at 1× scale. A wrong shard key means an online migration of everything; a wrong consistency choice means a product redesign. And then there's the organizational stage: at 100×, the operational surface — hundreds of instances, deploys, on-call — becomes the dominant constraint, and that's where cells, progressive delivery, and strong on-call processes start paying for themselves. The design gets *simpler*, not more complex, as scale increases, because cell isolation lets you reuse a simple design 64 times."

practice.afterTopic: The scoring rubric interviewers actually use
items: Latency of a main-memory access? 🟢 ~100 ns. (DRAM is ~100× slower than L3 — the cliff.)
Latency of an SSD random read? 🟢 ~50–100 μs (NVMe; spinning disk is 1–10 ms).
Latency of a same-DC RPC? 🟢 ~0.1–1 ms including serialization — roughly 1000× a local call.
Cross-continent RTT? 🟢 ~70–150 ms. Physics: light in fiber travels at ~2/3 c.
Postgres indexed point query? 🟢 ~1–5 ms (~10 ms if it touches disk).
Redis GET, same region? 🟢 ~0.5–1 ms.
What is Little's Law? 🟢 Concurrency = throughput × latency. Turns latency into connection counts.
Why does p99 matter more than p50? 🔴 At 10k QPS, 1% is 100 req/s — errors become a product problem.
Why is latency nonlinear near 100% utilization? 🔴 Queueing: M/M/1 latency ≈ service time / (1 − ρ).
What is "overload collapse"? 🔴 Past the knee, added load *reduces* throughput; more servers can hurt.
Default load-balancing algorithm you'd use? 🟡 Least outstanding requests, behind L7 with outlier detection.
L4 vs L7 load balancer? 🟡 L4 for throughput and non-HTTP/long-lived; L7 for path routing, TLS, caching, WAF.
What is slow start on a load balancer? 🟡 Ramp traffic to newly healthy targets so cold instances aren't overloaded.
Liveness vs readiness probe? 🟢 Liveness = "restart me?" (dependency-free). Readiness = "route to me?"
Why must liveness not check the database? 🔴 A DB blip restarts the whole fleet → connection storm → worse outage.
What is outlier detection? 🟡 LB evicts a per-endpoint statistical outlier on observed errors/latency.
Sharding modulus problem? 🟡 hash % N: going N→N+1 remaps nearly all keys → full offline migration.
Consistent hashing move cost? 🟢 ~1/N of keys on add or remove.
Why virtual nodes? 🟡 Vanilla consistent hashing gives uneven arcs; vnodes concentrate each node's share near 1/N.
Rendezvous / HRW hashing vs consistent hashing? 🔴 No ring to maintain; provably minimal key movement; O(N) hashes per lookup.
What is a hinted handoff? 🟡 A neighbour accepts writes for an unavailable node and later forwards them.
Read repair? 🟡 On read, the coordinator overwrites stale replicas with the newest value.
Anti-entropy / Merkle trees? 🔴 Periodic full comparison of replicas to repair divergence read repair misses (cold data).
Sharding key for a feed app? 🟡 user_id — co-locates a user's data, matches the dominant query.
What does a hot key look like? 🔴 One celebrity with 10M followers → one shard/key at 100k QPS.
Mitigate a hot key? 🟡 Split the keyspace for that tenant, cache at the edge, per-key replica fan-out, sample.
Range vs hash partitioning? 🟢 Range = time-bounded queries + instant retention; hash = even writes, no range scans.
Why partition by time? 🟢 DROP PARTITION for retention is instant; DELETE of billions of rows is not.
Read replica lag typical? 🟡 0–2 s idle; seconds under load; can be minutes during failover.
Read-your-writes implementation? 🟡 Primary routing for a window, per-user sticky route, or min_version + replica wait.
What does stale-while-revalidate do? 🟡 Serve stale immediately, refresh in background. Turns cache into availability.
What does stale-if-error do? 🟡 Serve stale if the origin errors — pure availability insurance.
Cache-aside vs write-through? 🟢 Cache-aside (lazy, app reads on miss) is the default; write-behind risks data loss.
Three cache pathologies? 🟢 Stampede (thundering herd), penetration (nonexistent keys), avalanche (mass expiry).
Probabilistic early expiration? 🟡 Recompute expiry as exp − delta·rand()%K to stagger natural expiry.
What is a connection proxy? 🟡 PgBouncer/ProxySQL multiplex thousands of client connections onto few backends.
Postgres connection target per core? 🟡 Roughly 2–4× cores, not "as many as possible."
PgBouncer transaction-mode restriction? 🟡 No session state: no LISTEN/NOTIFY across txns, temp tables, held advisory locks.
Cross-shard uniqueness? 🔴 Becomes unique-within-shard; needs a global index or application-level enforcement.
What is a fan-out-on-read vs fan-out-on-write feed? 🟡 Write = precompute inboxes (fast reads, expensive writes). Read = merge at read time.

practice.title: Drill 1 — Photo app: read/write QPS
practice.afterTopic: The scoring rubric interviewers actually use
items: Question
The lesson
practice.reference:
```
ASSUMPTIONS (state these aloud):
  - 10M DAU
  - Feed page = 50 items → 4 feed loads/user/day (already given by "200 photos/day")
  - 1 feed load = 1 API request that internally fans out (see note)
  - Upload rate given: 0.2/user/day
  - Peak-to-average for a global product: ~3×
  - Design headroom: 2× peak

READ:
  Reads/day     = 10M users × 4 pages = 4 × 10^7 page loads/day
  Average RPS   = 4 × 10^7 / 86,400 ≈ 460 QPS
  Peak RPS      = 460 × 3 ≈ 1,400 QPS
  Design target = 1,400 × 2 ≈ 2,800 read QPS at the edge

  ⚠ The trap: "200 photos/day" is not 200 API calls. It's 4 calls returning 50 items each.
    If the implementation is 50 separate calls per page, it's 200 calls/user/day =
    2×10^7/day = 231 QPS avg, 700 peak — and that's a *worse* architecture, not a smaller system.
    Always ask: how many round trips?

WRITE:
  Writes/day    = 10M × 0.2 = 2 × 10^6 photos/day
  Average WPS   = 2 × 10^6 / 86,400 ≈ 23 writes/sec
  Peak WPS      = 23 × 3 ≈ 70; with a viral event, design for ~500

DECISIONS (the actual answer):
  - Read path is 40× the write path → read replicas + aggressive caching are worth it;
    write path can stay on a single writer for a long time.
  - 2,800 read QPS: ~10 app instances at ~300 RPS each with 2× headroom. Trivial.
  - The system is NOT compute-bound. It's storage- and bandwidth-bound (see Drill 3).
```
